newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU sees movement on controversial company law.
newsitem.headline: EU sees movement on controversial company law.

text.p: The European Commission voiced optimism on Thursday about prospects for progress on a draft EU corporate law allowing firms to set up as European companies, saying both Germany and Britain had moved on the complex issue.
The European Union executive's proposal for a European company statute, designed to make life easier and save costs for industry, has been deadlocked for more than 20 years.
The main stumbling block has concerned worker involvement in company decisions, an issue where London and Bonn have held fundamentally conflicting views.

But EU internal market ministers had "a very interesting debate" on Wednesday on a report of a high-level expert group suggesting ways out of the impasse, said Elisabetta Olivi, spokeswoman for EU Internal Market Commissioner Mario Monti.
"And on this basis the work on the European company statute will be relaunched," Olivi told journalists.
"We can certainly see that there is a change when compared to the past," she said, referring to the position of some EU states, notably Germany and Britain.
However, an EU diplomat stressed that more detailed discussion was needed and that some countries doubted whether the new report would form the basis for a breakthrough.
While Germany said at the meeting it had "nothing negative" to say about it, the position of Britain's new Labour government was still unclear, diplomats said.

The company statute would allow a firm to set up as a 'European company' operating on a Europe-wide basis and subject to EU rules applicable in all 15 member states, eliminating the need for companies to set up a network of costly subsidiaries.

The main conflict has involved provisions on worker participation in company decisions, with Bonn promoting its own system of "co-determination" between employees and managers and London arguing there should be no mandatory rules.

Seeking to resolve the row, a group headed by Etienne Davignon, the chairman of Belgian holding company Societe Generale and a former European commissioner, last week proposed that unions and employers should first try to agree on the worker involvement for each European company.
Only in the absence of agreement would a set of reference rules apply, covering information and consultation as well as participation of workers in company bodies.
British minister for European trade and competitiveness, David Simon, signalled at Wednesday's meeting that London was willing to "play a positive role" in further talks.

But he also said there was a need to be "realistic about the acceptability of any co-determination requirement on companies in countries where such provisions were not an existing feature of corporate governance."
EU diplomats said it was too early to say whether the new Labour government, which has said it will sign up to the EU social chapter, would make it easier to find agreement.

"Yes, there is now a Labour government but if it makes practical differences on this question, that is something we just have to see," one diplomat said, noting that Simon had not seemed "very enthusiastic".
Germany's lack of criticism may reflect the fact that the proposals were "more or less based on the German system," another EU diplomat said.
The issue will next be discussed by EU social affairs ministers meeting on June 12.
